analysis.one_liner: Moves large interstate class action lawsuits from state to federal courts and adds consumer protections on settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, received one hearing in July 2002, and died without ever getting a vote when Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let big class action lawsuits — cases over $2 million involving people from more than one state — be heard in federal court instead of state court. It would also require judges to closely review settlements where class members get coupons while their lawyers get cash, ban extra payouts to the named plaintiffs who file a case, and require plain-language notices that disclose how much lawyers plan to charge. Sponsors said state courts were biased against out-of-state companies; opponents said federalizing these cases would make it harder for consumers to sue national corporations.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, large companies facing class action lawsuits — banks, insurers, manufacturers, retailers — would benefit most, because they could move cases out of state courts and into federal court, which is generally slower and less favorable to plaintiffs. Class members would also get some real protections: judges would have to scrutinize coupon settlements before approving them, class representatives could not take extra 'bounty' payments, and settlement notices would have to disclose the attorney fees being requested.

how_it_helps.text: Federal courts would get original jurisdiction over class actions exceeding $2 million where plaintiffs and defendants are from different states, and any defendant could remove such a case to federal court without the consent of the other parties [S2][S3].

Judges could approve a noncash or coupon settlement only after a hearing and written finding that it is fair, reasonable, and adequate for class members, and could not approve a settlement that leaves a class member with a net loss to pay class counsel [S2][S3].
Settlements could not pay class members differently based on how close they live to the courthouse, and could not give the named class representative a larger share than everyone else [S3].
Settlement notices would have to open with a bold plain-language warning and disclose, among other things, the dollar amount of attorney fees being sought and how those fees would be calculated [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The main cost would fall on plaintiffs' class action attorneys, who would lose the ability to keep big national cases in state courts where they have historically fared better, and on state courts and state officials, who would lose jurisdiction over large cases and receive new settlement-notification paperwork. Corporate defendants would bear the modest cost of stricter judicial scrutiny of coupon-style settlements.

drawbacks.text: Moving class actions to federal court would make it harder for consumers to sue national companies in the state courts where class members live; any single defendant could force removal to federal court, and a judge's order sending a case back to state court could be appealed, adding delay [S3].

The bill treats large groups of separately injured people as a class for jurisdiction purposes and lets their claims be aggregated to reach the $2 million threshold, pulling more cases into a federal system that moves more slowly than many state courts [S3].

Its consumer protections address real abuses — lawyers collecting large fees while class members receive coupons — but the bill does not change the underlying legal claims, so its help for class members is procedural rather than substantive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill packaged genuine consumer protections against lawyer-favoring coupon deals with a major procedural win for corporate defendants: federal jurisdiction over big class actions. How you weigh it depends on whether you think federal courts or state courts better protect people suing big companies — that was the whole fight. The settlement-disclosure and coupon-review provisions stand on their own merit; the jurisdiction shift is the provision with the largest practical effect, and it runs in the direction companies wanted.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in November 2001, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, given a single hearing in July 2002, and left there — no committee vote, no floor vote — when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on November 15, 2001, with original cosponsors from both parties, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S3][S5].
The committee held hearings on the bill on July 31, 2002 [S5].
That was the last action taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plaintiffs' class action attorneys and the state-court status quo are better off because the bill died — big consumer cases stayed in state courts. Consumers gained nothing from its death but also never received its proposed protections against coupon settlements and unclear notices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plaintiffs' attorneys; state-court status quo held

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Class Action Fairness Act of 2001 and led its Senate support.

for.name: 18 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, 15 Republicans and 3 Democrats; original cosponsors included Democrats Herb Kohl and Thomas Carper and Republicans Orrin Hatch, Strom Thurmond, Lincoln Chafee, and Arlen Specter.

for.name: Business coalitions and large corporate defendants
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed class action 'reform' moving large cases to federal court, an agenda pursued in this era by business groups including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (chair Patrick Leahy)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; Democrats held the Senate majority
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on July 31, 2002, but never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a committee vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Plaintiffs' trial lawyers
against.role: Attorneys' bar that brings consumer class actions
against.what_they_did: Opposed federalizing class actions, arguing it would let corporations move consumer cases into a less favorable federal forum.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Republican and its 18 cosponsors split 15 Republicans to 3 Democrats; no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape never got tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Large corporate defendants (banks, insurers, manufacturers, retailers)
industries.note: The jurisdiction provisions would let any defendant move a $2 million-plus interstate class action into federal court without other defendants' consent, a forum companies have historically found safer. The bill's stated findings cite state-court bias against out-of-state defendants [S3]. The bill also gives banks and other depository institutions special regulator-notification channels for settlement notices [S3].

Federal removal, appealable remand orders, and new settlement-notification duties would raise the cost and risk of big consumer class actions, where these attorneys work mostly on contingency. Their ability to bring these cases is also how consumers recover money from national companies.

State courts would lose jurisdiction over most large interstate class actions, and state attorneys general and regulators would receive mandatory settlement notifications and a 90-day waiting period before final approval. This shifts consumer cases out of the forum closest to the people involved.
